```csharp
ctx.DrawVoxelSprite(model, mats, x: 12, baseY: 18, scale: 2.0,
                    alpha: 1.0, flip: false, shade: c => light.Apply(c));
```

### Voxel Models

A voxel model written as text, rendered through an orthographic iso camera with
Lambert light, hard shadows and ambient occlusion. The text format is the point:
it is small enough to author (or edit) inside a pixogram, and the same files
drive the voxel tools in the pxl-clock repo.

```csharp
var model = VoxModel.Parse("""
    material sand top=#F4E0A0 front=#A89060 side=#705D40   // side optional -> front
    material palm top=#5A8E32 front=#365A1E
    box 0 0 0  8 0 6  sand      # inclusive cuboid: x1 y1 z1  x2 y2 z2  material
    v 4 1 3 palm                # single voxel; later lines override earlier cells
    """);
// Coordinates: x right, y UP, z into the scene. model.Min / model.Max / Contains.

var cam = new IsoCamera { YawDegrees = 344, PitchDegrees = 334, Scale = 1.5 };
cam.PanX = 0; cam.PanY = 2;         // screen pan; LongAxisPan = -1..1 travels a wide model

ctx.DrawVoxModel(model, cam, VoxelLight.Golden());          // over the scene, alpha, shade hook
ctx.DrawVoxModel(model, cam, light, shade: c => fog.Apply(c, wz, nearZ, farZ, hazeColor));

// Lights: StudioRight (default), StudioLeft, Noon, Golden, Overcast, Moonlit -
// or derive it from the scene's own sun, so sky and model agree:
var light = VoxelLight.FromSkyBody(sun.At(cycle), canvasWidth: ctx.WidthF);
// Ambient, Direction, Intensity, Tint, Shadows, AmbientOcclusion are all settable.

// Bridges into the rest of the toolkit:
var mask = model.ToMask(cam, 24, 24);          // silhouette -> DrawRimLight / DrawHalo / DrawDropShadow
var targets = model.ToTargets(cam, 24, 24, light);   // rendered pixels -> PixelAssembly
var (sx, sy, depth) = model.Project(cam, 4.0, 8.5, 3.0, 24, 24);  // voxel point -> screen overlay

// Faces re-sort every frame. For a static shot, render once into a BakedSurface:
baked.Ensure(key, s => s.DrawVoxModel(model, cam, light));
```

### Debug Map

A top-down map of the world. On 24x24 this is the only practical way to check
navigation, collision or streaming logic, because the scene view hides most of
the world.

```csharp
var map = new DebugMap(ctx, worldHalfWidth: 26, worldDepth: 26,
                       background: Color.FromRgb(0.03, 0.07, 0.12));
map.Frustum(camera, Colors.SlateGray);
map.Disc(wx, wz, worldRadius: 1.6, Colors.Green);      // footprint
map.Ring(wx, wz, worldRadius: 4.0, Colors.Yellow);     // clearance
map.Line(boatWx, boatWz, targetWx, targetWz, Colors.DimGray);
map.Marker(boatWx, boatWz, Colors.Red, size: 2);
map.Camera(Colors.White);
map.ToCanvas(wx, wz);
```

### Trails, Transitions and Panel Colour

The canvas is CLEARED before every frame, so a motion trail cannot be made by
"not clearing" - it needs a buffer that survives, declared outside the scene.

```csharp
var trail = new TrailBuffer(24, 24, decay: 0.85);   // outside scene

// A) paint INTO the trail
trail.Decay();
trail.Surface.PlotAA(x, y, Colors.HotPink);
trail.Draw(ctx, BlendMode.Plus);

// B) echo the canvas (phosphor)
trail.Decay();
ctx.DrawSurface(trail.Surface, blendMode: BlendMode.Plus);
DrawScene(ctx);
trail.Capture(ctx, strength: 0.6);

trail.DecayTo = Color.FromRgb(0.05, 0, 0.1);   // decay toward a colour, not to nothing
trail.Clear();
```

Changing picture: a cut reads as a glitch, a transition reads as intent. All of
them take two surfaces and a progress u in [0, 1].

```csharp
Transitions.Fade(ctx, from, to, u);
Transitions.Wipe(ctx, from, to, u, angleDegrees: 20, softness: 2);
Transitions.Iris(ctx, from, to, u, centerX: 12, centerY: 12, softness: 1.5);
Transitions.Dissolve(ctx, from, to, u);          // stable hash order, never flickers
Transitions.ColumnFall(ctx, from, to, u);        // like a departure board
Transitions.Push(ctx, from, to, u, angleDegrees: 90);
```

Impact and rumble - deliberately NOT a filter, so the picture stays sharp:

```csharp
var (dx, dy) = Shake.At(sinceImpact, amplitude: 1.5, duration: 0.35);
var (rx, ry) = Shake.Rumble(t, amplitude: 0.6);
```

The panel is seen from two metres in a living room, which eats dark tones and
fine steps:

```csharp
Led.EnsureVisible(color, floor: 0.12);   // keep a silhouette off pure black
Led.Quantize(color, levels: 16);         // preview what the panel can separate
Led.Gamma(color, 2.2);
Led.BayerThreshold(x, y);                // stable 4x4 ordered dither threshold
Led.DitherMix(a, b, t, x, y);            // mix WITHOUT a muddy mid tone
```

### Warp, Glitch and CRT

Geometric filters read from the finished picture, so they work on anything -
text, sprites, a whole scene.

| Filter | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `Filters.Warp((x, y) => (srcX, srcY))` | free inverse mapping; the base of all of these |
| `Filters.Displace(field, strengthX, strengthY, seconds)` | push pixels along a field - heat shimmer, water, a flag |
| `Filters.Twirl(centerX, centerY, strengthDegrees, radius)` | whirlpool, portal, spin-up |
| `Filters.Ripple(centerX, centerY, wavelength, amplitude, phase, falloff)` | rings from a drop, sonar, shockwave |
| `Filters.Pixelate(size)` | chunky blocks - "zoomed out", censored |
| `Filters.ChromaticAberration(offsetX, offsetY)` | channel split - screen, hologram, damage |
| `Filters.Scanlines(strength, period, horizontal, offset)` | CRT rows |
| `Filters.Glitch(seed, intensity, bands, maxShift)` | bands jump sideways plus a flash line |
| `Filters.Threshold(level, high, low)` | two-tone, maximum readability |
| `Filters.Outline(color, alphaThreshold, diagonal)` | one-pixel outline around solid pixels |
| `Filters.Dither(levels)` | ordered dithering instead of banding |

Drive the glitch seed in STEPS (`(int)(t * 10)`) so the damage re-rolls in jumps
instead of crawling - that is what makes it read as a broken signal.

### Shapes: Profiles, Blobs and Ground

Three ways to build a body that primitives alone cannot draw. All three are
QUERYABLE, so one definition drives fill, shading, labels and dissolves.

```csharp
// A body described by its half-width per ROW: bottles, vases, rockets, towers
var bottle = new ProfileShape(centerX: 12, rows: new (double Y, double HalfWidth)[]
{
    (3, 1.6), (7, 1.4), (11, 5.4), (20, 5.4), (22, 4.6),
});
bottle.Fill(ctx, (x, y, edge) => ColorOps.Lerp(glass, glassEdge, edge * edge));
bottle.HalfWidthAt(y); bottle.Contains(x, y); bottle.EdgeFactor(x, y);
bottle.InBand(x, y, fromY: 13, toY: 18, inset: 1.0);    // a label band
bottle.ToTargets(24, 24, shade);                        // for a PixelAssembly

// Overlapping ellipse lobes with an irregular outline: canopies, clouds, foam
var canopy = new BlobField(
    new Blob(12, 8, 5.5, 4.2), new Blob(7, 10, 4.0, 3.4)) { Lumpiness = 0.22 };
canopy.Fill(ctx, (x, y, lobe, dx, dy, rim) =>
    rim < 0.3 ? ColorOps.Lerp(leaf, Colors.Black, (0.3 - rim) / 0.3) : leaf);
canopy.Sample(x, y);       // Value >= 0 inside, Index = owning lobe
canopy.Contains(x, y);

// A plane in perspective without world coordinates: roads, rails, furrows
var ground = new GroundPlane { HorizonY = 9, NearY = 24, VanishX = 12 };
ground.DepthAt(y);                               // 0 at the horizon, 1 at the feet
ground.ScaleAt(y);
ground.LaneCenterAt(y, nearX: 18);               // converges to the vanishing point
ground.LaneHalfWidthAt(y, nearHalfWidth: 6);
ground.CrossLine(y, spacing: 0.16, scroll: -t);  // sleepers / markings coming at you
ground.DepthLine(x, y, count: 8);                // furrows running INTO the depth
```

### Motion: Paths, Steering, Physics

```csharp
// Walk a polyline by DISTANCE: worms, rails, orbits, labels on a curve
var loop = new Path2D(closed: true, (5, 6), (19, 5), (20, 17), (12, 21));
var (x, y) = loop.At(distance);          loop.AtFraction(0.25);
loop.TangentAt(distance);                loop.AngleAt(distance);
loop.DrawTrail(ctx, head, segments: 8, spacing: 1.6, colorOf: i => ..., radius: 0.9);

// Velocities you add to your own state - nothing is simulated behind your back
Steering.Seek(px, py, tx, ty, maxSpeed);
Steering.Arrive(px, py, tx, ty, maxSpeed, slowRadius);
Steering.Avoid(px, py, cx, cy, radius, strength);
Steering.Wander(seconds, seed, speed);

// The tests steering needs
Geometry.Distance(ax, ay, bx, by);
Geometry.InDisc(px, py, cx, cy, r);
Geometry.ClosestOnSegment(px, py, ax, ay, bx, by);
Geometry.SegmentClearOfDisc(ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, r, margin);
Geometry.PushOutOfDisc(px, py, cx, cy, r);   // hard constraint: never inside

// Closed form, so the scene can ask "when does it land" before it starts
Ballistics.FallTime(distance, gravity);
Ballistics.FallDistance(t, gravity);
Ballistics.Throw(x0, y0, vx, vy, t, gravity);
Ballistics.BounceHeight(t, dropHeight, gravity, restitution);

// Weight without a state machine: overshoots slightly, settles, never snaps
var follow = new Spring(12.0, stiffness: 8.0, damping: 0.7);   // outside scene
var v = follow.Step(ctx, target);

// Hard constraints - apply AFTER integration; "never inside", whatever forces did
Geometry.PushOutOfAabb(px, py, minX, minY, maxX, maxY);
Geometry.PushOutOfSegment(px, py, ax, ay, bx, by, radius);
```

### Force Fields and Verlet

A force is a field: direction + strength per position. One field can drive
particles, a rope, an agent and a filter at the same time - that is what makes
wind read as ONE weather instead of three separate effects.

```csharp
var wind = VectorField.Sum(
    VectorField.Constant(8.0, -1.0),                       // steady breeze
    VectorField.Curl(scale: 0.18, strength: 9, driftSpeed: 1.1));  // gusts (divergence-free)
VectorField.Swirl(cx, cy, strength, radius);               // whirlpool / vortex
VectorField.Attract(cx, cy, strength, radius);             // magnet; negative repels
VectorField.Gradient(scalarField, strength);               // uphill of any IScalarField
VectorField.From((x, y, t) => (vx, vy));                   // your own

embers.Force = wind;                                       // particles ride it
var (vx, vy) = Steering.Flow(px, py, wind, t, maxSpeed);   // an agent rides it
ctx.Filter(Filters.Displace(wind, strength: 0.8, seconds: t)); // a layer rides it

// Verlet: points + distance links. Ropes, chains, pendulums, flags, soft
// bodies - stable, tiny, and far more readable on 24x24 than rigid bodies.
var rope = VerletSystem.Rope(4, 2, 4, 19, segments: 12, pinStart: true);
rope.Force = wind;
rope.Constrain = p => (p.X, p.Y) = Geometry.PushOutOfDisc(p.X, p.Y, 15, 14, 4);
var flag = VerletSystem.Grid(7, 4, cols: 7, rows: 5, spacing: 1.9,
    pin: (cx, cy) => cx == 0);                             // shear-stiff by default
foreach (var _ in sim.Steps(ctx)) rope.Step(1.0 / 30, t);  // FIXED steps (FixedStep)
foreach (var (a, b) in rope.Links) ctx.DrawGlowLine(a.X, a.Y, b.X, b.Y, core, glow);
// rope.Points[i].X/Y to draw; move a pinned point by hand to drag the rope.
```

### Cellular Automata

The cheapest source of endless non-repeating content: rules instead of frames.

```csharp
var life = new CellGrid(24, 24);              // outside scene; byte per cell
life.Randomize(0.32, seed: 7);
life.StepLife();                              // Conway
life.Step((x, y, self, n) => n == 3 || (self != 0 && n == 2) ? (byte)1 : (byte)0);
life.Draw(ctx, (x, y, v) => v == 0 ? null : ColorOps.Lerp(cool, warm, life.CountNeighbours(x, y) / 6.0));

var sand = new CellGrid(24, 24, wrap: false);
sand.SeedFrom(logoSurface, alphaThreshold: 0.4, value: 1);   // start from a picture
sand.StepSand();                                             // grains fall and pile
```

Step the automaton on its OWN clock (6-15 steps per second), not once per frame -
40 steps per second is far too fast to read.

### Weather, Fog and Stars

Stateless layers: every particle is derived from its index and the time, so
nothing is stored and nothing drifts out of sync.

```csharp
var rain = Weather.Rain(intensity: 0.8);      // or Weather.Snow(...), Weather.Embers(...)
rain.Wind = -6; rain.FloorY = 18;             // flat floor: stop at one row
rain.FloorFarY = horizonY; rain.FloorNearY = 23.5;  // PERSPECTIVE floor: far drops
rain.Splash = 2.5;                            // land at the horizon, near ones at the
                                              // bottom, each with a brief impact blip

// Weather is LIT like everything else - derive its colour from the scene's
// light each frame, or night rain glows on top of the picture:
rain.Color = light.Apply(Color.FromRgb(0.65, 0.80, 1.00), minAmbient: 0.25);
rain.Draw(ctx, t);

var fog = new FogBank { CenterY = 12, Thickness = 4, Density = 0.5, Speed = 1.2 };
fog.Color = light.Apply(Color.FromRgb(0.80, 0.85, 0.92), minAmbient: 0.22);
fog.Draw(ctx, t);

var stars = new StarField { Density = 0.05, TwinkleSpeed = 0.8 };
stars.Draw(ctx, t, visibility: cycle.Night, maxY: (int)horizonY);
```

Every field of `Precipitation` is public - Count, Speed, SpeedSpread, Wind, Sway,
Streak, Color, Alpha, DepthSpread, FloorY, SwaySpeed, Seed - so ash, confetti and sparks are the
same class with different numbers. `DepthSpread` staggers the drops into depth
layers (far ones fall slower, dimmer, with shorter streaks) - that parallax is
what makes rain read as a volume instead of a single sheet.

### Typography and Clocks

```csharp
// Glyphs as rows of '#' and '.', drawn pixel exact
var font = PixelFont.FromRows(3, 5, new Dictionary<char, string[]>
{
    ['P'] = ["###", "#.#", "###", "#..", "#.."],
});
PixelFont.Digits3x5.Draw(ctx, "12:45", 2, 9, Colors.White);
PixelFont.Digits3x5.DrawCentered(ctx, "42", 9, Colors.White);
font.Measure(text); font.ToTargets(text, x, y, color);   // -> PixelAssembly
var info = font.ToFontInfo();   // now works with every DrawText* helper
ctx.DrawTextOutlined("42", 3, 9, info, Colors.White);    // outlined custom glyphs

// Text that arrives over time
TextMotion.Typewriter("HELLO", seconds, charsPerSecond: 5);
var (offset, total) = TextMotion.Marquee(textWidth, 24, seconds, pixelsPerSecond: 7, gap: 4);
// Offset starts at -canvasWidth: the first pass slides in from the right edge.

// A clock that rolls over like an odometer instead of snapping
var roll = new RollingText();                 // outside scene
roll.Update(ctx.Now.ToString("HHmmss"), t);
var (offset, from, to) = roll.At(index, t, duration: 0.28);
```

### Sub-pixel Plotting and Light Beams

```csharp
// Splits a point over neighbouring pixels: the cure for "everything snaps"
ctx.PlotAA(x, y, color, alpha);

// A line whose row varies per column, sub-pixel accurate: horizons, water
// lines, hill crests, graphs
ctx.DrawRowLine(x => horizonY + wave.Value(x, horizonY, t) * 0.3, color, 0.8);

// The glitter path a light leaves on water - a cone of broken highlights,
// which is what makes water read as water
var beam = new SpecularBeam { SourceX = moonX, TopY = waterY, Length = 10 };
beam.Draw(ctx, waveField, t, beamColor, sparkColor, intensity: 0.9);
```

### Masks, Rim Light and Shadow

A mask is a per-pixel coverage map: "where is my subject". It is what lets you
light, outline, halo and ground something WITHOUT knowing how it was drawn.

```csharp
var before = ctx.Snapshot();
DrawSubject(ctx);
var subject = Mask.FromDiff(before, ctx);     // what did I just draw?

subject.DrawDropShadow(ctx, offsetX: 1.5, offsetY: 2.0, strength: 0.45);
subject.DrawRimLight(ctx, warmColor, directionDegrees: -55, strength: 0.75);
subject.DrawHalo(ctx, coolColor, radius: 2, strength: 0.30);
```

That trio - shadow, rim, halo - is the difference between a sticker and an
object in a scene, and it costs three lines.

```csharp
Mask.FromAlpha(surface, threshold);        Mask.FromLuminance(surface, threshold);
Mask.FromPredicate(w, h, (x, y) => ...);   sprite.ToMask(24, 24, x, y);
mask.EdgeOutside(radius);  mask.EdgeInside();  mask.Grow(1);  mask.Shrink(1);  mask.Invert();
mask.Paint(ctx, color, alpha);             mask.Paint(ctx, (x, y, cov) => color);
mask.Contains(x, y);
```

Shading formulas that turn a flat fill into a body:

```csharp
Shading.Cylinder(t, lightAt: 0.35);            // across a trunk, a pipe, a limb
Shading.Sphere(dx, dy, lightX, lightY);        // off-centre highlight = a ball
Shading.Contact(x, y, centerX, groundY, rx, ry); // the shadow that grounds an object
Shading.Sway(heightFactor, seconds, amplitude, speed, phase); // wind, two sines
Shading.Ridge(x, baseY, amplitude, roughness, seed);          // mountain silhouette
```

### Sprites Written as Text

A figure authored directly in the source - no asset file, no loader, readable in
a diff. Any character missing from the table (by convention '.') is transparent.

```csharp
var cat = PixelSprite.FromRows(new[]
{
    ".g....g.",
    "gggggggg",
    "gwgggwgg",
    ".gyyyyg.",
}, new Dictionary<char, Color>
{
    ['g'] = Color.FromRgb(0.42, 0.38, 0.45),
    ['w'] = Colors.White,
    ['y'] = Color.FromRgb(0.85, 0.70, 0.35),
});

cat.Draw(ctx, x, y, alpha: 1.0, flipX: true, tint: fogColor, tintStrength: 0.4);
cat.DrawScaled(ctx, x, y, scale: 2);
cat.ToMask(24, 24, x, y);      cat.ToTargets(x, y);

var walk = new SpriteAnimation(framesPerSecond: 6, frameA, frameB, frameC);
walk.Draw(ctx, t, x, y, flipX: false);
```

### Gauges, Perimeter and Scrim

Ways to show a value that read from two metres - a number does not.

```csharp
ctx.DrawBarGauge(x, y, width, height, value, fill, frame, background);
ctx.DrawRingGauge(cx, cy, radius, value, fill, track, thickness);
ctx.DrawDotRow(x, y, count: 6, lit: 3, onColor, offColor, spacing: 2);

// The canvas border as a clock face: one turn = one full ring
var ring = new PerimeterPath(24, 24, inset: 0);
ring.DrawTicks(ctx, 12, tickColor, 0.5);
ring.DrawArc(ctx, ctx.Now.Second / 60.0, color, 0.85);
var (x, y) = ring.AtValue(ctx.Now.Second, 60);       // where the "hand" is
var (px, py) = ring.AtFraction(0.25);

// Text over a busy scene needs help: a scrim keeps the picture visible underneath
ctx.DrawScrim(y: 17, height: 6, strength: 0.45);
ctx.DrawTextContrast(ctx.Now.ToString("HH:mm"), 4, 18, Fonts.Var4x5, alpha: 0.9);
```

### Timing: Fixed Steps, Triggers and Rare Events

```csharp
// A simulation at its OWN rate. 40 automaton steps per second are unreadable.
var sim = new FixedStep(stepsPerSecond: 8);        // outside scene
foreach (var _ in sim.Steps(ctx)) grid.StepLife();

// Fires exactly on the frame a value changes - "the second ticked over"
var tick = new ChangeTrigger<int>();               // outside scene
if (tick.Changed(ctx.Now.Second)) sparks.Burst(...);
tick.Previous;   // the value before the change - e.g. the digit a roll starts from

// Rare events on a stable schedule with jitter - lightning, a shooting star,
// a bird. Deterministic, so nothing has to be remembered.
var flash = Slots.Progress(t, slotSeconds: 7.0, chance: 0.55, duration: 0.35, seed: 3);
if (flash >= 0) ctx.Filter(Filters.Fade(Colors.White, (1 - flash) * (1 - flash) * 0.5));
Slots.Index(t, 7); Slots.Local(t, 7); Slots.Value(t, 7, seed); Slots.Active(t, 7, 0.5, 0.3);
```

### Colour on a Small Panel

```csharp
ColorOps.LerpHsl(a, b, t);      // takes the SHORT way round the wheel - no mud
color.ShiftHue(0.08);           color.Complement();
ColorOps.ToHsl(color);

palette.SampleDithered(t, x, y);  // ordered dithering INSTEAD of blending:
                                  // a four-colour ramp stays four colours and
                                  // still reads as a smooth gradient
Filters.Grain(seed, strength);    Filters.ChannelRotate(steps);
```

### Echoes, Glow and Plotted Functions

```csharp
// An analytic motion trail: the same draw callback for earlier points in time.
// No buffer, no state - the trail comes from the motion function itself.
ctx.DrawEcho(t, count: 6, step: 0.05, (s, time, alpha) =>
    s.DrawCircle(PosX(time), PosY(time), 2, colorFill: Colors.Cyan.WithAlpha(alpha)));

// Three concentric discs read as light; one disc reads as a circle.
ctx.DrawGlow(x, y, radius: 4, color, layers: 3, coreAlpha: 0.9);

// A function plotted as a connected line: graphs, skylines, terrain, heartbeats
ctx.DrawFunctionLine(x => Shading.Ridge(x, 17, 4, 1, seed: 2), ridgeColor, 0.9);
```

### Envelopes, Falloffs and Micro-drawing

An easing goes from A to B. An ENVELOPE goes up, holds and comes back - which is
what a flash, a spark, a pop or a gust actually does.

```csharp
Envelope.Bell(p);                       // sin(p*pi) - the one-beat effect
Envelope.Spike(p, power: 4);            // a sharper bell
Envelope.RampHold(p, attack: 0.2, release: 0.3);
Envelope.Life(p, fadeIn: 0.15, fadeOut: 0.35);   // exactly 0 at both ends: loop-safe
Envelope.Anticipate(p);                 // dips back, overshoots, settles
Envelope.Pulse(t, period: 1.2, duty: 0.25);
Envelope.Twinkle(t, speed: 2, power: 8);// mostly dim, brief flares - stars, glints
```

FALLOFFS - how something fades with distance:

```csharp
Falloff.Gauss(distance, sigma);         Falloff.Linear(distance, radius);
Falloff.Smooth(distance, radius);
Falloff.Ring(distance, radius, width);  // EMPTY in the middle: shockwaves, portals
Falloff.Cone(across, depth, widthBase, widthGrow);   // a beam on a surface
```

MOTION shapes and frame timing:

```csharp
MotionShape.Arc(x0, y0, x1, y1, u, bulge);   // travel on a curve, not a straight line
MotionShape.SquashStretch(amount);           // volume-preserving scale pair
var clock = new FrameClock();  var dt = clock.Delta(ctx);   // measured, capped
```

MICRO-DRAWING - below about two pixels the normal primitives snap from cell to
cell. These work at sub-pixel accuracy, which is what lets small things MOVE:

```csharp
ctx.PlotAA(x, y, color, alpha);                  // one point, sub-pixel
ctx.PlotDiscAA(x, y, radius, color, alpha);      // a 1.5-pixel dot that glides
ctx.DrawSparkle(x, y, brightness, color, diagonal: true);
ctx.DrawGlowLine(x0, y0, x1, y1, core, glow, coreWidth: 0.6, glowWidth: 3.0);
ctx.DrawTextOutlined(text, x, y, Fonts.Var4x5, color, outline: Colors.Black);
ctx.Filter(Filters.RollingScanline(position, width, strength));
```

### SkiaSharp Interop (Advanced)

The Pxl renderer is built on SkiaSharp internally, but the regular API hides every Skia type. When you need a Skia construct that no Pxl factory exposes (composed shaders, runtime SKSL, custom blend modes, exotic tile modes), opt in via the **`Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Advanced`** namespace. The namespace itself signals "I'm coupling to SkiaSharp now".

```csharp
using Pxl.Ui.CSharp;
using Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Advanced;   // ← required for any of the helpers below
using SkiaSharp;                 // ← required for SK* types
```

**Conversions (extension methods in `SkiaInterop`):**

```csharp
// Color ↔ SKColor
SKColor sk = Colors.Red.ToSkia();
Color px = new SKColor(0xFF, 0x80, 0x00).ToPxl();

// BlendMode ↔ SKBlendMode
SKBlendMode skMode = BlendMode.Plus.ToSkia();
BlendMode pxMode = SKBlendMode.Lighten.ToPxl();

// Typeface → SKTypeface (for custom Skia text APIs)
SKTypeface tf = Fonts.Var4x5.Typeface.ToSkia();
```

**Custom shaders as paints (via `AdvancedPaints.Shader`):**

```csharp
var shader = SKShader.CreateLinearGradient(
    new SKPoint(0, 0), new SKPoint(24, 24),
    new[] { Colors.Red.ToSkia(), Colors.Blue.ToSkia() },
    SKShaderTileMode.Mirror);
ctx.DrawCircle(12, 12, 10, colorFill: AdvancedPaints.Shader(shader));
```

This unlocks the full SkiaSharp catalogue — perlin noise with custom seeds, image shaders, composed shaders, runtime SKSL shaders, etc.

**Note:** the regular `Pxl.Ui.CSharp` namespace contains its own `TileMode` enum (`Clamp`/`Repeat`/`Mirror`/`Decal`) and a `Transform2D` struct (`Identity`/`Translate`/`Scale`/`Rotate`/`Skew`/`Then`) that all gradient and image-pattern paints accept directly — you only need the Advanced namespace for things Skia exposes that Pxl doesn't.

---

```xml
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterLayer">
            <summary>
            An offscreen surface bound to a parent: draw onto it like any surface, give
            it a transform, then <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterLayer.Apply(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Interpolation,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter)"/> composites it onto the parent.
            Create one via <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurfacePixelExtensions.NewLayer(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Int32,System.Int32)"/> (empty)

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterLayer.Apply(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Interpolation,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter)">
            <summary>
            Composites the layer onto its parent - the second half of the layer
            workflow (draw isolated, then Apply). The optional
            <paramref name="filter"/> runs on the layer alone first, then the pixels
            travel through the layer transform and are blended with
            <paramref name="blendMode"/>. That scoping is the point: a blur or glow
            stays inside the layer instead of smearing the whole canvas.
            <paramref name="interpolation"/> only matters when a transform resamples.
            </summary>
        </member>

            <summary>
            A layer that starts as a copy of this surface - the way to post-process
            what is already drawn: fork, mutate or filter the copy, then
            <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterLayer.Apply(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Interpolation,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter)"/> composites it back (with

            For drawing NEW isolated content start empty with <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurfacePixelExtensions.NewLayer(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Int32,System.Int32)"/>.

            </summary>

            <param name="x1">The x-coordinate of the first corner.</param>
            <param name="y1">The y-coordinate of the first corner.</param>
            <param name="x2">The x-coordinate of the opposite corner.</param>
            <param name="y2">The y-coordinate of the opposite corner.</param>
            <param name="colorFill">The fill paint (solid color, gradient, etc.). If null, no fill is drawn.</param>
            <param name="colorStroke">The stroke paint (solid color, gradient, etc.). If null, no stroke is drawn.</param>
            <param name="strokeWidth">The width of the stroke.</param>
            <param name="isAntialias">Whether to use anti-aliasing.</param>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RoundedRectExtensions.DrawRoundedRect(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PaintOrColor},System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PaintOrColor},System.Double,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            Draws a rectangle with rounded corners.
            </summary>
            <param name="ctx">The drawing context.</param>

            <param name="isAntialias">Whether to use anti-aliasing.</param>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ProfileShape">
             <summary>
             A body defined by its half-width per row - a bottle, a vase, a rocket, a
             tree trunk, a lighthouse. Instead of assembling primitives you describe the
             silhouette once and then ask it what belongs to the shape.
            
             This is what makes a hand-drawn object look designed rather than assembled:
             the outline is authored row by row, and everything else (fill, label band,
             highlight, glass) reads from the same profile.
            
             <code>
             var bottle = new ProfileShape(centerX: 12, rows: new (double Y, double HalfWidth)[]
             {
                 (2, 2.0), (4, 2.4), (6, 1.9), (9, 5.6), (12, 6.0), (21, 6.0), (22, 5.3),
             });
             bottle.Fill(ctx, (x, y, edge) => ColorOps.Lerp(glass, glassEdge, edge * edge));
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ProfileShape.#ctor(System.Double,System.ValueTuple{System.Double,System.Double}[])">
            <summary>
            Creates a profile from control rows. Rows are interpolated linearly, so
            a handful of points is enough; anything outside the first and last row is
            not part of the shape.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ProfileShape.CenterX">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField">
             <summary>
             A soft body made of overlapping ellipse lobes - tree canopies, cloud banks,
             bushes, smoke, foam. Each pixel belongs to the nearest lobe in normalised
             distance, and the lobe outline is modulated by a couple of sine terms so the
             silhouette is irregular instead of a row of circles.
            
             The field value is what makes it useful: it is positive inside, near zero at
             the rim, so the same call gives you fill, rim darkening and a dissolve mask.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.#ctor(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Blob[])">
            <summary>Creates a blob field from its lobes.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.Lumpiness">
            <summary>How strongly the lobe outlines are modulated (0 = clean ellipses).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.Blobs">
            <summary>The lobes.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.Sample(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Samples the field: greater than 0 inside the body, around 0 at the rim,
            negative outside. Also reports which lobe owns the pixel and where the
            pixel sits inside it, which is what shading needs.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.Contains(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>True when the pixel is inside the body.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlobField.Fill(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color}})">
            <summary>
            Fills the body. The callback gets the pixel, the owning lobe index, the
            offset inside that lobe and the rim distance (0 at the silhouette, larger
            toward the middle) - enough for volume shading, dappled light and a
            darkened outline. Return null to skip a pixel.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GroundPlane">
             <summary>
             A ground plane seen in perspective: rows below the horizon map to depth, and
             anything laid out on the plane (a road, furrows, a lane of markings, a grid)
             converges toward a vanishing point.
            
             This is the flat cousin of <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera"/>: no world coordinates,
             just "how does a plane look from here" - which is what most 2.5D scenes need.
             </summary>
        </member>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.DrawTaperedLine(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Double,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Draws a line whose width tapers from start to end, shaded across its
            width. The building block for branches, trunks, cables, smoke trails
            and anything organic that a plain stroke makes look flat.
            </summary>

            <param name="taper">How much the width shrinks toward the end (0 = none, 1 = to zero).</param>
            <param name="colorLo">Colour at the left edge of the limb.</param>
            <param name="colorHi">Colour at the right edge of the limb.</param>
            <param name="shadeBias">Shifts the light/dark split across the width (0.5 = centred).</param>
            <param name="steps">Sampling steps along the limb. 0 picks a sensible value from the length.</param>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.FillSupersampled(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Func{System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color}},System.Int32,System.Double)">
             <summary>
             Fills an area from a procedural shape function with supersampled
             anti-aliasing: the function is asked <paramref name="samples"/> squared
             times per pixel and the results are averaged.
            
             This is how a rotated, hand-built sprite (a boat with a tilted mast, a
             swinging pendulum) gets smooth edges without a rasterizer.
             </summary>
             <param name="ctx">The drawing context.</param>
             <param name="minX">Left edge of the area to test.</param>
             <param name="minY">Top edge of the area to test.</param>
             <param name="maxX">Right edge of the area to test.</param>
             <param name="maxY">Bottom edge of the area to test.</param>
             <param name="sample">Returns the colour at a sub-pixel position, or null for "not part of the shape".</param>
             <param name="samples">Sub-samples per axis (4 = 16 per pixel).</param>
             <param name="edgeBoost">Multiplier on the coverage: values above 1 keep interiors fully opaque and only soften the outermost edge.</param>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.DrawScrim(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.DrawVoxelSprite(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Voxel},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelMaterial},System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean,System.Func{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
             <summary>
             Draws a voxel model in oblique cabinet projection: depth shifts a cube
             up on the canvas, every cube paints a lit top face and a shaded front
             face, and the model is sorted back-to-front so it occludes itself
             correctly.
            
             This is the quick 2.5D sprite mode - fixed view, two colours per
             material. For a real orbiting camera, directional light, shadows and
             ambient occlusion use <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel"/> with an
             <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera"/> and <c>DrawVoxModel</c>.
            
             Voxel coordinates: x to the right, y up from the base, z into the scene.
             </summary>
             <param name="ctx">The drawing context.</param>
             <param name="voxels">The model.</param>
             <param name="materials">Material table; <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Voxel.Material"/> indexes into it.</param>
             <param name="x">Screen x of the model centre.</param>
             <param name="baseY">Screen y of the model's base row.</param>
             <param name="scale">Canvas pixels per voxel.</param>
             <param name="alpha">Overall opacity.</param>
             <param name="flip">Mirrors the model horizontally.</param>
             <param name="shade">Optional per-colour transform, e.g. lighting or haze.</param>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.PlotAA(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Plots a point at a sub-pixel position by splitting its weight over the
            neighbouring pixels. This is what lets a thing MOVE smoothly on a 24x24
            grid instead of jumping from cell to cell - the single most effective
            trick against the "everything snaps" look.
            </summary>
        </member>

            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SceneShapeExtensions.DrawEcho(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Action{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double},System.Double)">
            <summary>
            An analytic motion trail: the same draw callback is invoked for a few
            EARLIER points in time, with decaying alpha. No buffer, no state - the
            trail is derived from the motion function itself.
            <code>
            ctx.DrawEcho(t, count: 6, step: 0.05, (surface, time, alpha) =>
                surface.DrawCircle(PosX(time), PosY(time), 2, colorFill: Colors.Cyan.WithAlpha(alpha)));
            </code>
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam">
             <summary>
             The glitter path a light source leaves on moving water: a cone that widens
             with distance, a soft base beam and bright sparks on the wave crests.
            
             A reflection is not a mirrored disc - it is a column of broken highlights,
             and that is exactly what makes water read as water.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.SourceX">
            <summary>Screen x of the light source.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.TopY">
            <summary>Row where the beam starts, usually the horizon or water line.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.Length">
            <summary>How many rows the beam reaches down.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.WidthBase">
            <summary>Beam half-width directly under the source.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.WidthGrow">
            <summary>How fast the cone widens per row.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.BaseStrength">
            <summary>Opacity of the always-visible base beam.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.SparkleStrength">
            <summary>Opacity of the sparkles on wave crests.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.SparkleThreshold">
            <summary>Wave value above which a pixel sparkles.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.GlowThreshold">
            <summary>
            Wave value above which the middle glow layer kicks in. Between this and
            <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.SparkleThreshold"/> the water is lit but not yet flashing -
            that middle band is what gives a sun path its body.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField,System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Draws the beam with three layers - base, glow on the rising water and
            sparkle on the crests. Three layers read as a path of light; one reads as
            a stripe.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SpecularBeam.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField,System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Draws the beam. <paramref name="field"/> supplies the wave motion,
            <paramref name="beamColor"/> is the soft base and
            <paramref name="sparkColor"/> the crest highlight.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D">
             <summary>
             A rectangular view onto a (usually much larger) surface: which part of the
             world is shown, how far it is zoomed in, and how it is rotated.
            
             The canvas shows a window of <c>Width / Zoom</c> by <c>Height / Zoom</c>
             world pixels around (<see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.CenterX"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.CenterY"/>).
             Zoom 1 is 1:1, Zoom 4 magnifies four times, Zoom 0.25 shows four times
             as much world as the canvas has pixels.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.CenterX">
            <summary>World x the camera looks at.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.CenterY">
            <summary>World y the camera looks at.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.Zoom">
            <summary>Canvas pixels per world pixel. 1 = 1:1, greater = magnified.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.Rotation">
            <summary>Camera rotation in degrees (positive = world turns counter-clockwise).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.Focus(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Creates a camera looking at a world point with the given zoom.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.LerpTo(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Moves the camera a fraction <paramref name="t"/> from this pose toward
            <paramref name="target"/>. Zoom is interpolated geometrically so the
            motion feels linear at every scale.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D.WorldToScreen(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Maps a world point to canvas coordinates for the given canvas size.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface">
             <summary>
             A surface that is rendered only when its key changes - the "bake it once,
             then just copy it" pattern for expensive static content (a painted
             backdrop, a tree, a city skyline).
            
             Declare it OUTSIDE the scene lambda so it survives across frames.
            
             Warning: the internal <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Surface"/> has frozen time (Elapsed 0, Now
             at construction) - a render callback reading time from it silently gets
             constants; take time from the outer ctx instead.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.#ctor(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Creates an offscreen surface of the given size.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Surface">
            <summary>The offscreen surface. Valid after the first <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Ensure(System.Object,System.Action{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface})"/> call.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Ensure(System.Object,System.Action{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface})">
            <summary>
            Renders <paramref name="render"/> into the surface if <paramref name="key"/>
            differs from the key of the last bake. Returns true when a re-render happened.
            Pass any value that identifies the content (a variant index, a date, a tuple).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Invalidate">
            <summary>Forces the next <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface.Ensure(System.Object,System.Action{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface})"/> call to re-render.</summary>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid">
             <summary>
             A grid of cells that steps by a rule - Game of Life, falling sand, a spreading
             fire, a maze, rust, a growing crystal. On 24x24 a cellular automaton is one of
             the few things that produces genuinely new pictures forever without any
             authored content.
            
             The grid holds a byte per cell (0 = empty), so it works for both "alive/dead"
             and for multiple materials or ages. Declare it OUTSIDE the scene lambda.
             Seed convention: double seeds select stateless hash variants; int seeds
             seed a stateful Random.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.#ctor(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>Creates an empty grid.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Width">
            <summary>Grid width in cells.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Height">
            <summary>Grid height in cells.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Wrap">
            <summary>Whether neighbours wrap around the edges.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Generation">
            <summary>How often <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Step(System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Byte,System.Int32,System.Byte})"/> has run.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Item(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Reads or writes a cell. Out-of-bounds reads return 0.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Get(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Reads a cell, honouring <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Wrap"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.CountNeighbours(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Number of non-zero cells among the eight neighbours.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.CountNeighbours(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Byte)">
            <summary>Number of neighbours with a specific value.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Clear">
            <summary>Clears the grid.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Randomize(System.Double,System.Byte,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Fills the grid randomly with the given density (0..1).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Step(System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Byte,System.Int32,System.Byte})">
            <summary>
            Applies a rule to every cell simultaneously (double buffered, so a cell
            never sees a half-updated neighbourhood).
            <code>
            life.Step((x, y, self, n) => n == 3 || (self != 0 &amp;&amp; n == 2) ? (byte)1 : (byte)0);
            </code>
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.StepCells(System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Byte,System.Byte})">
            <summary>
            Applies a rule that only needs the cell and the grid (for automata that
            look at specific neighbours, like falling sand).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.StepLife">
            <summary>Conway's Game of Life, the classic rule as a one-liner.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.StepSand(System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Falling sand: non-zero cells fall down, or diagonally if blocked. Runs
            bottom-up in place, which is what makes grains stack instead of teleport.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Func{System.Byte,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color}},System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Draws the grid: the callback maps a cell value to a colour, null leaves the pixel alone.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Byte,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color}},System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Draws the grid with position-aware colouring (for age or height gradients).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.CellGrid.SeedFrom(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Byte)">
            <summary>Seeds the grid from a picture: every pixel above the alpha threshold becomes a cell.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode">
            <summary>
            Blend modes control how colors are combined when drawing on top of existing content.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Clear">
            <summary>
            Clear destination (replace with transparent).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Source">
            <summary>
            Replace destination with source.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Destination">
            <summary>
            Keep destination, ignore source.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.SourceOver">
            <summary>
            Source over destination (default alpha blending).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.DestinationOver">
            <summary>
            Destination over source.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.SourceIn">
            <summary>
            Source inside destination (mask source by destination alpha).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.DestinationIn">
            <summary>
            Destination inside source (mask destination by source alpha).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.SourceOut">
            <summary>
            Source outside destination (inverse mask).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.DestinationOut">
            <summary>
            Destination outside source (inverse mask).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.SourceAtop">
            <summary>
            Source atop destination (source where destination is opaque).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.DestinationAtop">
            <summary>
            Destination atop source (destination where source is opaque).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Xor">
            <summary>
            Exclusive OR (source XOR destination).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Plus">
            <summary>
            Add source and destination (clamps to 1.0).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Modulate">
            <summary>
            Multiply source and destination (darkens).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Screen">
            <summary>
            Screen blend mode (inverted multiply, lightens).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Overlay">
            <summary>
            Overlay blend mode (combination of multiply and screen).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Darken">
            <summary>
            Darken: keeps the darker of source and destination.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Lighten">
            <summary>
            Lighten: keeps the lighter of source and destination.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.ColorDodge">
            <summary>
            Color dodge (brightens destination based on source).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.ColorBurn">
            <summary>
            Color burn (darkens destination based on source).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.HardLight">
            <summary>
            Hard light (harsh version of overlay).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.SoftLight">
            <summary>
            Soft light (gentle version of overlay).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Difference">
            <summary>
            Difference (absolute difference between source and destination).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Exclusion">
            <summary>
            Exclusion (similar to difference but lower contrast).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Multiply">
            <summary>
            Multiply (darkens by multiplying colors).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Hue">
            <summary>
            Hue blend mode (use source hue with destination saturation and luminosity).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Saturation">
            <summary>
            Saturation blend mode (use source saturation with destination hue and luminosity).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Color">
            <summary>
            Color blend mode (use source hue and saturation with destination luminosity).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode.Luminosity">
            <summary>
            Luminosity blend mode (use source luminosity with destination hue and saturation).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps">
            <summary>
            Color blending and lighting operations. These complement the constructors
            on <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color"/> with operations BETWEEN colours - interpolation,
            tinting, lighting - that pixogram authors otherwise rewrite by hand.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.Lerp(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Componentwise linear interpolation between two colors. <paramref name="t"/>
            is clamped to [0, 1]: 0 returns <paramref name="a"/>, 1 returns <paramref name="b"/>.
            Alpha is also interpolated.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.LerpTo(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>Extension form of <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.Lerp(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.Tinted(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Mix this colour TOWARD another by <paramref name="strength"/> (0..1).
            Equivalent to <c>Lerp(this, tint, strength)</c> - useful for "warm tint at horizon"
            or "blend in a touch of ambient" effects.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.LitBy(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
             <summary>
             Multiplicative lighting: simulate the colour being lit by a coloured light
             at a given brightness. Returns componentwise <c>color x light x brightness</c>,
             clamped to [0, 1] per channel. Alpha is preserved.
            
             Example: a brown wood deck under cool blue moonlight at 40% brightness:
             <c>woodColor.LitBy(Color.FromRgb(0.45, 0.55, 0.85), 0.40)</c>.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.LerpHsl(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Interpolates in HSL and takes the SHORTER way around the colour wheel.
            An RGB lerp from red to green goes through mud; this one goes through
            orange and yellow, which is what a viewer expects.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.ShiftHue(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>Shifts the hue by a fraction of the wheel, keeping saturation and lightness.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.Complement(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color)">
            <summary>The colour opposite on the wheel - instant contrast that still belongs together.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.ToHsl(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color)">
            <summary>Hue, saturation and lightness of a colour, each in [0, 1].</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ColorOps.Blend(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color[],System.Double[])">
            <summary>
            N-way weighted blend. Returns the linear combination of the given colors
            using the given weights. Weights need not sum to 1 - they're normalised
            internally. If <paramref name="weights"/> is empty or all zero, returns
            the first color.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color">
            <summary>
            Represents a color with RGBA components.
            <para>
            The Color struct provides a double-based public API (0.0 to 1.0 range) while internally
            storing the color as a single <c>uint</c> in ARGB format.
            </para>
            <para>
            Factory methods and properties with "Byte" suffix work with byte values (0-255),
            while methods without suffix work with double values (0.0-1.0).
            </para>
            </summary>
            <remarks>
            <list type="table">
            <listheader><term>Property</term><description>Description</description></listheader>
            <item><term><see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.R"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.G"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.B"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.A"/></term><description>Color components as double (0.0-1.0)</description></item>
            <item><term><see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.RedByte"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.GreenByte"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.BlueByte"/>, <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.AlphaByte"/></term><description>Color components as byte (0-255)</description></item>
            </list>
            </remarks>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.R">
            <summary>Gets the red component as a value from 0.0 to 1.0.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.G">
            <summary>Gets the green component as a value from 0.0 to 1.0.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.B">
            <summary>Gets the blue component as a value from 0.0 to 1.0.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.A">
            <summary>Gets the alpha (opacity) component as a value from 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (opaque).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color.RedByte">
            <summary>Gets the red component as a byte value from 0 to 255.</summary>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope">
             <summary>
             Envelopes: the shape of an event over its lifetime. Easings go from A to B;
             an envelope goes UP, HOLDS and comes back DOWN - which is what almost every
             effect actually needs (a flash, a spark, a pop, a bubble, a gust).
            
             All of them take a progress p in [0, 1] and return a factor in [0, 1].
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Bell(System.Double)">
            <summary>Rises and falls symmetrically: sin(p * pi). The one-beat effect.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Spike(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>A sharper bell - a spark rather than a swell.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.RampHold(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Attack, hold, release. <paramref name="attack"/> and
            <paramref name="release"/> are fractions of the total; the rest is the
            hold. Smoothstepped at both ends.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Life(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            A life envelope built from two smoothsteps - fades in, lives, fades out,
            and is exactly 0 at both ends, so it is safe to loop.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Anticipate(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Anticipation, overshoot, settle: dips below 0 first, shoots past 1, then
            comes back. The curve that makes a movement look intentional.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Pulse(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            A repeating pulse: bright for a moment, then dark. <paramref name="duty"/>
            is the fraction of the period that is lit. Unlike the other members this
            takes absolute seconds and schedules itself.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Twinkle(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Twinkle: a sine raised to a power, so it spends most of its time dim and
            flares briefly. Far more convincing than a plain sine for stars, glints
            and fireflies. Like <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Envelope.Pulse(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)"/> it takes absolute seconds and
            schedules itself.
            </summary>
        </member>

            glows, beams, rings and soft edges - writing them by hand every time is where
            scenes start to look inconsistent.
            </summary>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Falloff.Linear(System.Double,System.Double)">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.DayCycle">
             <summary>
             The time of day as one small object: where in the 24h cycle we are and how
             much "day", "twilight" and "night" that means. Everything else in a
             day/night scene (sky palette, light, star visibility, clock overlay) should
             be derived from these factors instead of re-deriving the hour.
            
             Three sources, same interface:
             <code>
             var cycle = DayCycle.FromClock(ctx);                       // production
             var cycle = DayCycle.Animated(ctx, secondsPerDay: 24.0);   // preview / GIF
             var cycle = DayCycle.Fixed(18.5);                          // study one moment
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.DayCycle.FromClock(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface)">

        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody">
             <summary>
             A sun, a moon or any other body travelling an elliptic arc over the scene.
             At phase 0 the body sits at the left of its ellipse, climbs to the top a
             quarter cycle later, and sets on the right.
            
             A moon is just a second body with <c>PhaseOffset = Math.PI</c> - antipodal,
             so it rises exactly when the sun sets.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody.CenterX">
            <summary>Screen x of the arc centre.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody.CenterY">

        </member>

        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody.AmpY">
            <summary>Vertical radius. Larger means the body climbs higher (possibly out of frame).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody.PhaseOffset">
            <summary>Phase shift in radians. <c>Math.PI</c> makes a body antipodal to the sun.</summary>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient">
             <summary>
             The sky as a gradient with THREE horizon colours instead of one: warm where
             the sun stands, cool where the moon stands, and a far colour everywhere else.
             Each pixel mixes toward a body's colour by its horizontal distance to it.
            
             This is what makes a sunset look like a sunset. A single horizon colour gives
             an even orange wash across the whole sky; the pull gives a warm COLUMN of
             light with cool sky beside it - and that contrast is the entire effect.
            
             The same call also colours the water: ask for <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.HorizonColorAt(System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.DayCycle,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBodyState},System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBodyState})"/>
             per column and use it as the near-water tone, so the glow continues below
             the horizon instead of stopping at it.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.Top">
            <summary>Colour at the top of the sky.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.Horizon">
            <summary>Horizon colour away from any celestial body.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.SunHorizon">
            <summary>Horizon colour right below the sun - the warm one.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.MoonHorizon">
            <summary>Horizon colour right below the moon - the cool one.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGradient.HorizonY">

        </member>

            spot.

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow">
             <summary>
             The atmospheric rendering of a sun or moon: a sharp core, a bright glow and a
             wide halo - and, as the body sinks, an ellipse that stretches sideways.
            
             The stretch is what sells a low sun: a round disc reads as a lamp, a smeared
             one reads as light through kilometres of air. The other half is timing - the
             glow keeps burning for a while after the core has set, which is why a sunset
             has an afterglow at all.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.Core">
            <summary>The bright centre.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.Glow">
            <summary>The inner glow around the core.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.Halo">
            <summary>The wide, faint halo.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.CoreRadius">
            <summary>Radius of the sharp core in pixels.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.CrispCore">
            <summary>True draws the core as a crisp anti-aliased disc (moon), false as a soft gaussian (sun).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyGlow.GlowSigma">
            <summary>Width of the inner glow.</summary>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.DebugMap">
             <summary>
             A top-down map of a world for debugging: where objects really are, where an
             actor is heading, and what the camera can see. On 24x24 this is the only
             practical way to check navigation and collision logic, because the scene
             view itself hides most of the world.
            
             Draw it instead of the scene while debugging:
             <code>
             var map = new DebugMap(ctx, worldHalfWidth: 25, worldDepth: 30);
             map.Disc(island.Wx, island.Wz, 2.0, Colors.Green);
             map.Ring(island.Wx, island.Wz, 6.0, Colors.Yellow);
             map.Frustum(camera, Colors.SlateGray);
             map.Marker(boat.Wx, boat.Wz, Colors.Red, size: 2);
             </code>
            
             Deliberately the only block that binds ctx in its constructor - it is a
             debug tool, not a scene building block.
             </summary>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera">
             <summary>
             A pinhole camera over a ground plane - the cheapest way to get real depth
             on a 24x24 canvas. World points are (wx, wz): wx is lateral, wz is distance
             from the camera. The camera sits at height <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera.Height"/> above the
             plane and looks along +z.
            
             <code>
             var cam = new PinholeCamera { Height = 1.6, Focal = 24, HorizonY = 10 };
             var p = cam.Project(wx, wz);        // p.X, p.Y, p.Scale
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera.Height">
            <summary>Camera height above the ground plane in world units.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera.Focal">

        </member>

        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera.CenterX">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WorldStream">
             <summary>
             A lateral drift stream past the camera: objects keep a fixed depth, drift
             sideways over time, fade over an off-frame band and recycle to the far end
             of the track once they leave it. Good for panning past islands, clouds,
             trees along a road, a skyline.
            
             It does NOT move anything toward the viewer - there is no z motion, so
             "flying into the scene" needs its own wz animation.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WorldStream.Speed">
            <summary>Lateral world units per second the world drifts (positive = objects move left).</summary>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer">
             <summary>
             A persistent buffer that keeps what was drawn in earlier frames and dims it
             a little every frame - motion trails, phosphor glow, light painting, comet
             tails, matrix rain.
            
             The canvas itself is cleared before every frame, so a trail CANNOT be made
             by simply not clearing. Declare the buffer OUTSIDE the scene lambda; it is
             the only thing that survives.
            
             Two ways to use it:
             <code>
             // A) paint INTO the trail: the buffer is the drawing surface
             trails.Decay();
             trails.Surface.DrawCircle(x, y, 2, colorFill: Colors.Cyan);
             trails.Draw(ctx, BlendMode.Plus);
            
             // B) echo the CANVAS: draw the scene normally, then feed it to the buffer
             trails.Decay();
             ctx.DrawSurface(trails.Surface, blendMode: BlendMode.Plus);
             DrawScene(ctx);
             trails.Capture(ctx, 0.6);
             </code>
            
             Warning: the internal <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Surface"/> has frozen time (Elapsed 0, Now
             at construction) - anything reading time from it silently gets constants;
             take time from the outer ctx instead.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.#ctor(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double)">
            <summary>Creates a trail buffer of the given size.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Surface">
            <summary>The buffer you can draw into.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.DecayFactor">
            <summary>
            How much of the previous content survives one <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Decay"/>:
            0.85 is a medium tail, 0.95 a very long one, 0.5 a short smear.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.DecayTo">
            <summary>Colour the trail decays toward. Transparent (default) fades out.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Decay">
            <summary>Dims the stored content by <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.DecayFactor"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Decay(System.Double)">
            <summary>Dims the stored content by an explicit factor.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Capture(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)">
            <summary>Copies the current canvas into the buffer, weighted by <paramref name="strength"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TrailBuffer.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BlendMode,System.Double)">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Transitions">
             <summary>
             Transitions between two pictures. The second half of a storyboard: a scene
             change that is a WIPE, an IRIS or a DISSOLVE reads as intent, while a plain
             cut reads as a glitch.
            
             All methods take two surfaces and a progress u in [0, 1] and draw the result
             onto the canvas.
             </summary>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Led">

            shades become indistinguishable.

            still reads once the display eats the fine steps.
            Same maths as <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Posterize(System.Int32)"/>, applied to a single
            colour instead of a whole layer.

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Led.Dither(System.Double,System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Ordered (Bayer 4x4) dithering: turns a smooth value into a stable
            two-level pattern. On a low-bit panel a dithered gradient reads smoother
            than a quantised one, and the pattern never flickers because it depends
            only on the pixel position.
            </summary>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Led.Gamma(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
```
