        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField">
             <summary>
             A travelling wave field: several sine trains stacked, optionally warped and
             crossed so the fronts are not perfectly straight. Sample it as a number and
             use it for anything that ripples - water, flags, fog banks, grain fields,
             a mirror distortion.
            
             The point of having it as an object is that ONE field can drive many things
             at once (surface colour, foam, reflections, how a boat rolls), and they all
             stay in sync automatically.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Octaves">
            <summary>Number of sine octaves in the main direction (1..4).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.FrequencyX">
            <summary>Spatial frequency of the first octave along x.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.FrequencyY">
            <summary>Spatial frequency of the first octave along y.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Speed">
            <summary>Travel speed of the first octave.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Gain">
            <summary>Amplitude falloff per octave.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Lacunarity">
            <summary>Frequency growth per octave.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.CrossStrength">
            <summary>Strength of the counter-running wave train (0 = pure 1D look).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.DomainWarp">
            <summary>How strongly the fronts are bent (0 = straight lines).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.OriginY">
            <summary>Row from which the field is measured - usually the horizon.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.PerspectiveSquash">
            <summary>
            Perspective compression: rows farther from <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.OriginY"/> get
            stretched, so a wave surface seen at a shallow angle reads correctly.
            0 disables it.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Value(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Samples the field. Result is roughly in [-2, 2], typically within [-1.6, 1.6].</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.SlopeX(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Horizontal slope of the field - drives roll angles and lighting.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.SlopeY(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Vertical slope of the field.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Normal(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Surface normal derived from the slopes, normalised.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField.Crest(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Crest strength in [0, 1]: 0 below the threshold, rising as the wave peaks.
            The direct input for foam, glitter and highlights.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ScalarField">
            <summary>
            Adapters that turn any function or noise into an <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField"/>,
            so it can feed everything a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField"/> can: a mirror's
            distortion, a displacement filter, a specular beam. Consumers expect fields
            roughly centred on 0 (a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField"/> swings about +/-1.5), which
            is exactly what these adapters produce.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ScalarField.From(System.Func{System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double})">
            <summary>Wraps a plain (x, y, seconds) function as a field.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ScalarField.Noise(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Drifting fractal noise as a field, centred on 0: values in
            [-amplitude, +amplitude], drifting with time. The turbulence counterpart
            to a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField"/>'s regular swell.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IVectorField">
            <summary>
            A direction and strength per position - the force counterpart to
            <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField"/>. Wind, currents, whirls and attractors all
            implement this one interface, so a particle field, a verlet rope, a
            steering agent and a displacement filter can share the SAME force source
            and automatically agree with each other.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IVectorField.Vector(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Samples the field at a position and time in seconds.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField">
            <summary>
            Factories for common force fields, and <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Sum(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IVectorField[])"/> to compose them:
            a breeze plus a whirl plus a repelling obstacle is one field, and everything
            driven by it stays in sync.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.From(System.Func{System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.ValueTuple{System.Double,System.Double}})">
            <summary>Wraps a plain (x, y, seconds) function as a field.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Constant(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>A uniform force - wind, a current, sideways gravity.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Swirl(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            A whirl around a centre: tangential flow, strongest near the centre,
            smoothly fading to 0 at <paramref name="radius"/>. Positive strength
            turns counter-clockwise.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Attract(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Pulls toward a centre (negative strength pushes away), fading to 0 at
            <paramref name="radius"/>. Attractors, repelling obstacles, a magnet.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Curl(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Divergence-free turbulence from noise (curl noise): the flow swirls and
            drifts but never piles up or drains away - THE field for smoke, embers,
            drifting snow and underwater particles.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Gradient(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            The gradient of a scalar field, scaled: points uphill. Feed it a
            <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField"/> and particles drift with the swell.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VectorField.Sum(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IVectorField[])">
            <summary>Adds several fields into one - composition is the whole point.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise">
            <summary>
            Value noise as a plain number - the counterpart to the Perlin paints, which
            can only be used as a fill. Deterministic: the same coordinates always give
            the same value, so textures never flicker between frames.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Value(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Smooth value noise in [0, 1] over a 2D position.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Value(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Smooth value noise in [0, 1] over a 3D position - use z for time.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Fbm(System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Fractal noise: several octaves of <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Value(System.Double,System.Double)"/> stacked.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Fbm(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Fractal noise over a 3D position - pass time as z for drifting textures.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Ridged(System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Ridged fractal noise - sharp crests, good for mountains and lightning.
            For a one-line mountain silhouette see <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Ridge(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)"/>.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Scatter">
            <summary>
            Deterministic scatter: which pixels get a star, a foam fleck, a blade of
            grass. Stable across frames because it is pure hashing, never a Random.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Scatter.Has(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>True when this pixel is part of a scatter of the given density (0..1).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Scatter.At(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Scatter strength in [0, 1]: 0 for pixels that are not part of the scatter,
            otherwise a value that ramps up with how far the pixel is past the
            threshold. Gives a natural brightness spread for free.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Scatter.Value(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Stable per-pixel random value in [0, 1) - for phases, sizes, hues.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Scatter.Pick(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double[])">
            <summary>
            Stable weighted choice per pixel: returns an index into
            <paramref name="weights"/>. Weights need not sum to 1.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter">
            <summary>
            A post-processing step that rewrites every pixel of a surface. Filters are
            meant to run on an isolated layer, not on the finished canvas, so an effect
            stays inside the layer it belongs to.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter.Apply(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface)">
            <summary>Applies the filter in place.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField">
             <summary>
             A field of doubles sampled per pixel - used by filters that need a spatial
             signal (ripples on a mirror, turbulence on a fade).
            
             Convention: consumers (<c>Filters.Mirror</c>, <c>Filters.Displace</c>,
             <c>SpecularBeam</c>) are calibrated for fields roughly CENTRED ON 0 - a
             <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.WaveField"/> swings about +/-1.5. Wrap a [0, 1] source (noise)
             with <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ScalarField"/> to centre and scale it.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField.Value(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Samples the field at a pixel position and time in seconds.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters">
             <summary>
             Post-processing filters for layers: blur, glow, edges, colour grading,
             vignette, glint and mirror.
            
             All filters work on the surface they are applied to, so the usual pattern is
             <c>layer.Apply(BlendMode.Plus, filter: Filters.Blur(1.5))</c> or
             <c>ctx.Filter(Filters.Vignette(0.4))</c>.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Chain(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IPixelFilter[])">
            <summary>Applies several filters in the given order.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Custom(System.Func{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>
            Free-form colour filter: maps every pixel through a function of its
            colour and position. The catch-all for tinting, channel swaps and
            hand-rolled effects.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Blur(System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Gaussian blur with the given radius in pixels. Alpha is respected
            (premultiplied), so blurring a transparent layer softens its edges
            instead of pulling in black.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Sharpen(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Unsharp mask: adds back the difference between the image and a blurred
            copy. Use sparingly at 24x24 - it quickly looks noisy.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Bloom(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Bloom: everything brighter than <paramref name="threshold"/> is blurred
            and added back on top. The natural way to make lamps, suns and neon
            glow instead of just being bright.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.EdgeDetect(System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            Sobel edge detection on luminance. With <paramref name="edgeColor"/> the
            edges are drawn in that colour, otherwise they keep the underlying hue.
            <paramref name="keepSource"/> false gives edges on black - an outline pass.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.ColorGrade(System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Colour grading: multiplicative tint, brightness, contrast around mid grey
            and saturation. The single dial set for "give the whole layer a mood".
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Levels(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Black/white point and gamma correction per channel.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Posterize(System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Quantises each channel to N steps - a poster / retro look.
            Same maths as <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Led.Quantize(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Int32)"/>, applied to a whole layer
            instead of a single colour.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Grayscale(System.Double)">
            <summary>Drops all colour, keeping perceived brightness.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Vignette(System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>
            Darkens toward the edges. <paramref name="radius"/> is the fraction of the
            half-diagonal that stays untouched.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Fade(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Blends the whole surface toward a colour - black for a cut, white for a
            flash, a blue-grey for fog or distance.
            A single-frame wash toward a colour, not a temporal fade - for a
            cross-fade over time see <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Transitions.Fade(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)"/>.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Glint(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask)">
            <summary>
            A bright band sweeping across the surface - glass, polished metal, a
            screen reflection. <paramref name="position"/> runs the band from the left
            edge (0) to the right edge (1); drive it from time. An optional
            <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask"/> confines the band to a subject, weighted by coverage.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Mirror(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Double,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Mirrors everything above <paramref name="atY"/> downward: water surface,
            glass table, wet asphalt. The reflection fades with distance, can be
            tinted, and an optional field (e.g. a <c>WaveField</c>) distorts it.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Grain(System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            Film grain: a per-pixel brightness jitter. A touch of grain makes flat
            gradients look like material instead of like a fill. Drive the seed from
            time (or leave it fixed for a still, dusty look).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.ChannelRotate(System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Rotates the colour channels (R-&gt;G-&gt;B). A one-line false-colour pass -
            useful for a "wrong signal" look or to reuse one scene in three moods.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Warp(System.Func{System.Double,System.Double,System.ValueTuple{System.Double,System.Double}},Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Interpolation)">
            <summary>
            Geometric warp: for every target pixel the function returns where to READ
            from (inverse mapping). All the warps below are built on this - use it
            directly for anything they do not cover.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Displace(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Pushes pixels sideways by a field - heat shimmer, water in front of a
            scene, a flag, a bad TV signal. Pass a <c>WaveField</c> or any other
            <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IScalarField"/>.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Displace(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IVectorField,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Displacement along a vector field: each pixel is pushed where the field
            points. The same wind that drives particles or a rope can smear a layer.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Twirl(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Rotates the image around a centre, more strongly toward the middle -
            a whirlpool, a portal, a spin-up.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Ripple(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Concentric rings running outward from a centre - a drop hitting water,
            a sonar ping, a shockwave.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Pixelate(System.Int32)">
            <summary>Chunky pixels: averages blocks of <paramref name="size"/>. Reads as "zoomed out" or "censored".</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.ChromaticAberration(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Splits the colour channels apart by a few pixels - a cheap lens error
            that instantly reads as "screen", "hologram" or "damaged signal".
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Scanlines(System.Double,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Darkens every other row (or column) - CRT look, and a good way to make a
            bright surface feel like a screen inside the scene.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Glitch(System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Signal breakup: a few horizontal bands jump sideways, the channels split
            and a bright line flashes. <paramref name="seed"/> should change over
            time (e.g. <c>(int)(t * 12)</c>) so the pattern re-rolls in steps rather
            than crawling.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.RollingScanline(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>
            A single bright band travelling down the picture, multiplicative - the
            rolling bar of an old tube. Position runs 0..1 over the height; drive it
            from time.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Threshold(System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>Everything above the luminance threshold becomes one colour, everything below another. Hard, graphic, very readable from a distance.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Outline(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            Draws a one-pixel outline around everything that is not transparent -
            the cheapest way to keep a subject readable in front of a busy
            background.
            Diagonal neighbours do not count by default - unlike
            <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.EdgeOutside(System.Int32,System.Boolean)"/>, which defaults to diagonal: true.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Dither(System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Ordered dithering to N levels per channel - keeps a gradient readable on
            a panel that cannot show the fine steps, without the banding that plain
            quantising produces.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FilterExtensions">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FontInfo">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxGlyph">
            <summary>
            One glyph of an Adafruit GFX bitmap font.
            Field semantics match the C <c>GFXglyph</c> struct.
            </summary>
            <param name="BitmapOffset">Byte offset into <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont.Bitmap"/> where this glyph's bits start.</param>
            <param name="Width">Glyph bitmap width in pixels.</param>
            <param name="Height">Glyph bitmap height in pixels.</param>
            <param name="XAdvance">How far to advance the cursor on x after drawing.</param>
            <param name="XOffset">X distance from the cursor to the glyph's upper-left corner.</param>
            <param name="YOffset">Y distance from the baseline to the glyph's upper-left corner (usually negative).</param>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont">
            <summary>
            An Adafruit GFX bitmap font. Unlike the vector (TTF/OTF) fonts, glyphs are
            stored as raw bitmaps: the <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont.Bitmap"/> bytes are packed MSB-first
            and read bit-by-bit, continuously across each glyph's <c>Width * Height</c>
            pixels (rows are NOT byte-aligned). A set bit is a lit pixel.
            The font data is transcribed to C# in <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFontData"/>.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont.Bitmap">
            <summary>All glyph bitmaps, concatenated. Indexed via <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxGlyph.BitmapOffset"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont.Glyphs">
            <summary>One entry per code point in <c>[First, Last]</c>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.GfxFont.First">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Hash">
            <summary>
            Deterministic pseudo-random hash functions. Same input -> same output every
            frame, every render, every device. Useful for placing things like stars,
            foam scatter, glitter etc. without needing a stateful Random.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Hash.From2D(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>

            hash: <c>fract(sin(dot(p, k)) * 43758.5453)</c>.
            </summary>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask">
             <summary>
             A per-pixel coverage map in [0, 1] - "where is my subject". Masks are what
             turn a drawn shape into something you can light, outline, halo, shadow or
             dissolve, WITHOUT knowing how it was drawn.
            
             The most useful way to get one is <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.FromDiff(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)"/>: take a snapshot,
             draw something, and ask what changed. From then on the subject can be
             rim-lit and haloed even though it was an arbitrary sequence of draw calls.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.#ctor(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Creates an empty mask.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Width">
            <summary>Mask width.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Height">
            <summary>Mask height.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Item(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Coverage at a pixel, 0 outside the mask.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.FromAlpha(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)">
            <summary>Everything on a surface with at least this alpha.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.FromLuminance(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)">
            <summary>Everything brighter than a luminance threshold.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.FromDiff(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            What changed between two states of a surface - the "what did I just
            draw" mask.
            <code>
            var before = ctx.Snapshot();
            DrawSubject(ctx);
            var subject = Mask.FromDiff(before, ctx);
            subject.DrawHalo(ctx, Colors.Gold, 2);
            </code>
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.FromPredicate(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double})">
            <summary>A mask from a predicate - circles, bands, anything analytic.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Contains(System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>True when a pixel is inside the mask.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.EdgeOutside(System.Int32,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            The outline: pixels just OUTSIDE the mask that touch it. This is what a
            silhouette rim, an outline and a halo are all built from.
            Diagonal neighbours count by default - unlike <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Filters.Outline(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double,System.Boolean)"/>,
            which defaults to diagonal: false.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.EdgeInside(System.Boolean)">
            <summary>The inner border: pixels of the mask that touch the outside.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Grow(System.Int32)">
            <summary>Grows the mask by a radius (dilate).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Shrink(System.Int32)">
            <summary>Shrinks the mask by a radius (erode).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Invert">
            <summary>Everything the mask does not cover.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Paint(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>Paints a colour wherever the mask covers, weighted by coverage.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.Paint(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color}})">
            <summary>Paints with a per-pixel colour callback.</summary>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.DrawHalo(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Int32,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            A soft glow around the silhouette, falling off over
            <paramref name="radius"/> pixels. Unlike a bloom this does not need the
            subject to be bright - a dark shape can have a rim of light behind it.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.DrawRimLight(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Lights the edge of the subject that faces a direction - the single most
            effective trick to make a flat silhouette look three-dimensional.
            The direction is in degrees, 0 = light from the right, -90 = from above.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask.DrawDropShadow(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Nullable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>
            Casts a shadow of the subject: the silhouette, shifted by the offset and
            blended darker into the background wherever the subject itself does not
            cover it. Sharp by design - no blur, just the offset copy.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading">
            <summary>
            Shading helpers - the small formulas that make a flat fill read as a solid
            body. They take a position and return a factor you multiply a colour by, so
            they compose with any palette.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Cylinder(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Cross-section shading for a cylinder: bright a third of the way in from
            the lit side, falling off to both rims. <paramref name="t"/> runs 0..1
            across the body.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Sphere(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Sphere shading from an off-centre highlight: 1 at the highlight, 0 at
            the far rim. dx, dy are the offsets from the centre, normalised by the
            radius.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Contact(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            A contact shadow under an object: an ellipse that is darkest right below
            it and fades outward. Nothing grounds an object faster.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Sway(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Wind sway offset: two sine terms of different periods, scaled by how far
            up the object a point sits (0 at the root, 1 at the tip). Vegetation
            that only uses one sine looks mechanical.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Shading.Ridge(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Layered ridge lines: a sum of sines that produces a mountain or hill
            silhouette for a column. Use one call per layer with different
            <paramref name="seed"/> and amplitude to get a parallax range.
            For an area texture with sharp crests (not a silhouette line) see
            <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Noise.Ridged(System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32)"/>.
            </summary>
        </member>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.MathH.Smoothstep(System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Smoothstep curve (Hermite interpolation): t^2 * (3 - 2t).
            Input clamped to [0, 1]. Slow start AND slow end, fast in the middle.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.MathH.Smootherstep(System.Double)">

            </summary>

             An ordered set of colour stops sampled by a normalised position t in [0, 1].
            
             Use a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette"/> when you need a colour-over-time or colour-over-
             value lookup - e.g. health bars, time-of-day tints, value-mapped heatmaps,
             fire-style flame gradients. Compare with <c>Paints.LinearGradient</c>, which
             fills a 2D shape with a gradient; <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette"/> returns a single
             <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color"/> per call.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.Colors">
            <summary>The colour stops, in order.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.Stops">
            <summary>
            The normalised positions [0..1] of each colour stop. If you constructed
            the palette without explicit positions, stops are evenly spaced.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.#ctor(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color[])">
            <summary>
            Creates a palette with evenly-spaced stops between the given colours.
            Two colours -> t=0 and t=1; three colours -> t=0, 0.5, 1; etc.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.#ctor(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color[],System.Double[])">
            <summary>
            Creates a palette with explicit stop positions. <paramref name="stops"/>
            must be the same length as <paramref name="colors"/>, sorted ascending,
            and within [0, 1].
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.Sample(System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Samples the palette at position <paramref name="t"/> in [0, 1].
            Returns the colour interpolated between the surrounding stops.
            Values outside [0, 1] clamp to the first/last colour.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.SampleWrapped(System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Samples the palette wrapping around - values outside [0, 1] wrap to a
            repeating cycle. Useful for periodic effects (rotating hue, looping fire).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palette.SampleDithered(System.Double,System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Samples the palette WITHOUT blending: the two neighbouring stops are
            mixed by ordered dithering instead. On a small panel this keeps the
            palette's colours crisp - a four-colour ramp stays four colours and still
            reads as a smooth gradient, which is exactly how hand-drawn pixel art
            shades a mass.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes">
            <summary>
            Built-in palettes for common use-cases.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Rainbow">
            <summary>Full-spectrum rainbow (red -> yellow -> green -> cyan -> blue -> magenta -> red).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Heat">
            <summary>Heatmap: cool blue -> green -> yellow -> red.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Fire">
            <summary>Fire/lava: black -> red -> orange -> yellow -> white.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Ice">
            <summary>Ice/glacier: deep blue -> ice blue -> frosted white.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Sunset">
            <summary>Sunset / golden hour: deep violet -> magenta -> orange -> gold -> pale yellow.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Grayscale">
            <summary>Greyscale ramp from black to white.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="F:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Palettes.Phosphor">
            <summary>Classic CRT phosphor green (black -> dark green -> bright green).</summary>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Param">
             <summary>
             Declares a tweakable parameter of a pixogram. Assign the result to a top-level
             variable and use that variable like an ordinary value - the compiler turns the
             declaration into a live-readable property, so changing the parameter from the app
             takes effect on the next frame.
             </summary>
             <example>
             <code>
             var speed = Param.Float(1.0, min: 0.1, max: 5.0);
             var count = Param.Int(5, min: 1, max: 20, label: "Star count");
             var glow  = Param.Bool(true);
             var tint  = Param.Color(Colors.Cyan);
             var mood  = Param.Choice("calm", ["calm", "lively", "wild"]);
            
             var scene = (RasterSurface ctx) =>
                 ctx.DrawCircle(ctx.Elapsed.TotalSeconds * speed, 12, count, tint);
             </code>
             </example>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Param.Float(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.String,System.String)">
            <summary>Declares a decimal number parameter.</summary>

            <param name="step">Increment, or 0 for continuous.</param>

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelTargets.NearestSources(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelTarget},System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{System.ValueTuple{System.Double,System.Double}})">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelAssembly">
             <summary>
             Animates a list of <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelTarget"/>s from a source point into their
             final position (or the other way round). Each pixel gets a launch angle and
             speed of its own, flies a short parabola and then settles onto its place.
            
             <code>
             var logo = new PixelAssembly(PixelTargets.From(logoSurface)) { Duration = 1.2 };
             logo.Draw(ctx, cue.LocalSeconds);          // assembles
             logo.DrawReverse(ctx, cue.LocalSeconds);   // falls apart
             </code>
            
             Seed convention: double seeds select stateless hash variants; int seeds
             seed a stateful Random.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelAssembly.#ctor(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelTarget},System.Int32)">

            <summary>
            Draws all particles. <paramref name="fadeOut"/> makes them dim as their
            life runs out; <paramref name="palette"/> optionally recolours them by
            remaining life (1 = fresh, 0 = gone). <paramref name="additive"/> adds
            single-pixel particles onto what is there (sparks over a scene); larger
            particles draw as anti-aliased discs and always composite normally.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint">
            <summary>
            One mass point of a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem"/>. Position is public state on
            purpose: a scene reads X/Y to draw, and may move a pinned point by hand
            (a hand holding a rope, an anchor riding a boat).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.#ctor(System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>Creates a point at rest.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.X">
            <summary>Current position.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.Y">
            <summary>Current position.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.PrevX">
            <summary>Position on the previous step - the velocity lives in the difference.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.PrevY">
            <summary>Position on the previous step.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletPoint.Pinned">
            <summary>A pinned point ignores forces and constraints and stays where it is put.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem">
             <summary>
             Verlet points plus distance constraints - ropes, chains, pendulums, flags
             and soft bodies in a handful of lines, and far more readable on 24x24 than
             exact rigid-body dynamics. Velocity is implicit (current minus previous
             position), which makes the integration unconditionally stable.
            
             Step it at a FIXED rate (<see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep"/>) - verlet assumes uniform
             steps, a variable frame delta makes it breathe.
            
             <code>
             var rope = VerletSystem.Rope(4, 2, 4, 16, segments: 9, pinStart: true);
             rope.Force = VectorField.Sum(VectorField.Constant(6, 0), VectorField.Curl());
             rope.Constrain = p => (p.X, p.Y) = Geometry.PushOutOfDisc(p.X, p.Y, 14, 12, 3.5);
             foreach (var _ in sim.Steps(ctx)) rope.Step(1.0 / 30, t);
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Points">
            <summary>The mass points, in insertion order.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Gravity">
            <summary>Downward acceleration in pixels per second squared.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Force">
            <summary>Optional force field (wind, whirls) - shared with particles and filters.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Retain">
            <summary>Velocity kept per step, 1 = frictionless. 0.985 is a calm rope.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Iterations">
            <summary>Constraint relaxation rounds per step. More = stiffer links.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Constrain">
            <summary>
            Hard per-point constraint, applied after the links every round - keep a
            point out of an obstacle (<see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Geometry.PushOutOfDisc(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)"/>), above a
            floor, inside the canvas. This is the rule that guarantees "never inside",
            no matter what the forces did.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Add(System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>Adds a point and returns it.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Link(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Nullable{System.Double})">
            <summary>
            Links two points (by index) with a distance constraint. Without an
            explicit <paramref name="length"/> the current distance is kept.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Links">
            <summary>The links as point pairs - for drawing the rope, chain or net.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Step(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Advances the simulation by one fixed step.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Rope(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            A rope from start to end, cut into <paramref name="segments"/> links.
            Pin one end and it hangs; pin neither and it falls.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VerletSystem.Grid(System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Double,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean},System.Boolean)">
            <summary>
            A cloth grid (a flag, a net): points linked to their right and lower
            neighbours, plus one diagonal per cell for shear stiffness - without it
            the cloth folds flat into a strip. <paramref name="pin"/> decides which
            points hold - e.g. <c>(cx, cy) => cx == 0</c> pins the left edge to make
            a flag.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelSprite">
             <summary>
             A sprite written directly in the source as rows of characters, with a
             character-to-colour table. No asset file, no loader, no path - the picture
             IS the code, which is exactly right for the handful of small figures a
             24x24 scene needs.
            
             <code>
             var dog = PixelSprite.FromRows(new[]
             {
                 ".bb..bb.",
                 "bwwwwwwb",
                 "bwkwwkwb",
                 ".bwwwwb.",
             }, new Dictionary&lt;char, Color&gt;
             {
                 ['b'] = Color.FromRgb(0.30, 0.18, 0.08),
                 ['w'] = Color.FromRgb(0.85, 0.75, 0.55),
                 ['k'] = Colors.Black,
             });
             dog.Draw(ctx, 8, 12);
             </code>
             Any character not in the table (by convention '.') is transparent.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelSprite.Width">
            <summary>Sprite width in pixels.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelSprite.Height">

            <summary>
            Draws the sprite with its top-left corner at (x, y).
            <paramref name="flipX"/> mirrors it - one sprite, two directions.

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Storyboard">
             <summary>
             A named sequence of timed segments - the dramaturgy of a scene in one place
             instead of a stack of hand-summed constants.
            
             <code>
             var story = new Storyboard(loop: true, seamFade: 0.5)
                 .Add("grow", 5.0).Add("fall", 2.4).Add("hold", 4.5);
            
             var cue = story.At(ctx);
             if (cue.Is("fall")) DrawFall(ctx, cue.Progress);
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep">
             <summary>
             A simulation that runs at its OWN rate, independent of the frame rate. Game
             of Life at 40 steps per second is unreadable; a falling-sand pile that only
             moves when the frame rate allows is unpredictable. Both want a fixed step.
            
             Declare it OUTSIDE the scene lambda.
             <code>
             var sim = new FixedStep(stepsPerSecond: 8);      // outside
             foreach (var _ in sim.Steps(ctx)) grid.StepLife();
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.#ctor(System.Double,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Creates a fixed-rate stepper.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.StepsPerSecond">
            <summary>How many simulation steps happen per second.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.MaxStepsPerFrame">
            <summary>Upper bound per frame, so a hitch cannot cause a burst.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.Count">
            <summary>How many steps have run in total.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.Due(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface)">
            <summary>How many steps are due this frame (and consumes them).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.Due(System.Double)">
            <summary>How many steps are due at an absolute time (and consumes them).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FixedStep.Steps(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface)">

        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.ChangeTrigger`1">
             <summary>
             Fires when a value changes - "the second just ticked over", "the minute
             flipped", "the variant changed". Without an edge trigger a scene either
             re-runs an effect every frame or misses it entirely.
            
             Declare it OUTSIDE the scene lambda.
             </summary>

            bird flying past, a glitch. The slot number is derived from time, so the

            <summary>Creates a rotation transform around a given pivot (in degrees).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Transform2D.Skew(System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Creates a skew transform (kx, ky in tangent units).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Transform2D.Then(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Transform2D)">
            <summary>Composes this transform with another, applied AFTER this one.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Typeface">
            <summary>
            An opaque handle to a loaded typeface. Pixogram authors don't construct
            these directly - use the predefined <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Fonts"/> entries.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont">
             <summary>
             A hand-set bitmap font: glyphs written as rows of '#' and '.', drawn pixel
             exact. When a scene needs three digits in a corner, or a wordmark that must
             hit exact pixels, a rasterised TTF is the wrong tool - this is authored at
             the pixel level and never surprises you.
            
             <code>
             var digits = PixelFont.FromRows(3, 5, new Dictionary&lt;char, string[]&gt;
             {
                 ['0'] = new[] { "###", "#.#", "#.#", "#.#", "###" },
                 ['1'] = new[] { ".#.", "##.", ".#.", ".#.", "###" },
             });
             digits.Draw(ctx, "10", 2, 3, Colors.White);
             </code>
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Width">
            <summary>Nominal glyph width.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Height">
            <summary>Glyph height.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Spacing">
            <summary>Pixels between two glyphs.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.FromRows(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary{System.Char,System.String[]},System.Int32)">
            <summary>Builds a font from a glyph table.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Digits3x5">
            <summary>
            The built-in 3x5 digit set - the smallest digits that stay unambiguous on
            an LED panel (closed loops on 0/6/8/9, an open notch on 4, a clear spine
            on 2/3/5). Includes ':' and '-'. For ordinary text prefer the rasterised
            fonts (<c>DrawTextMono3x5</c> etc.); reach for <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont"/>
            when you author custom glyphs or need <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.ToTargets(System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color)"/> or
            per-pixel colour.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Measure(System.String)">
            <summary>Width of a string in pixels.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Has(System.Char)">
            <summary>Whether a glyph exists.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>Draws a string with its top-left corner at (x, y).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Func{System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color},System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Draws a string with a per-pixel colour callback - the hook for gradients
            across a word, per-glyph colours or a flash on one digit. The callback
            gets the glyph index and the pixel position.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.DrawCentered(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.String,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)">
            <summary>Draws a string centred horizontally on the surface.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.ToFontInfo">
            <summary>
            Packs this font into a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FontInfo"/>, so hand-authored glyphs
            run on the standard text pipeline: <c>DrawText</c>, <c>DrawTextCentered</c>,
            <c>DrawTextOutlined</c>, <c>DrawTextContrast</c>, <c>MeasureText</c>.
            The drawing y is the top edge, exactly like <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,System.Double)"/>. The pen
            advances by the nominal <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Width"/> plus <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.Spacing"/>
            per glyph, matching this font's own layout.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelFont.ToTargets(System.String,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color)">
            <summary>Every lit pixel of a string as particle targets - for assemblies and dissolves.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TextMotion">
            <summary>
            Text that arrives over time instead of appearing at once: a typewriter with
            a blinking cursor, a marquee that scrolls, and digits that roll over like an
            odometer. On a 24x24 display these are the only honest ways to show more
            than four characters.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TextMotion.Typewriter(System.String,System.Double,System.Double,System.Boolean,System.Char,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            How much of a string is typed at a point in time, including a blinking
            cursor. Returns the substring to draw.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TextMotion.Marquee(System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Horizontal offset of a marquee: the text enters from the right edge,
            scrolls right to left and wraps with a gap. Draw the text at
            <c>-Offset</c> and again at <c>-Offset + Total</c> to get a seamless
            loop. Offset starts at <c>-canvasWidth</c>, so the first pass slides in
            instead of popping mid-screen.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TextMotion.DigitRoll(System.Char,System.Char,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Odometer roll: when a digit changes, the old one slides up and out while
            the new one slides in from below. Returns the sub-pixel offset and both
            characters, so a clock ticks over instead of snapping.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RollingText">
            <summary>
            Tracks when each character of a string last changed, so
            <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.TextMotion.DigitRoll(System.Char,System.Char,System.Double,System.Double)"/> can animate exactly the digits that
            ticked over. Declare it OUTSIDE the scene lambda.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RollingText.Update(System.String,System.Double)">
            <summary>Feeds the current text and the current time.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RollingText.At(System.Int32,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>Roll state of one character: offset 0 means settled.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel">
             <summary>
             A voxel model: a list of unit cubes plus a material table, parsed from the
             plain-text .vox format or built in code. The text format is the interesting
             part - it is small enough to write by hand (or by a model) inside a
             pixogram, and the same files drive the voxel tools in the pxl-clock repo.
            
             <code>
             var model = VoxModel.Parse("""
                 material sand  top=#F4E0A0 front=#A89060
                 material palm  top=#5A8E32 front=#365A1E
                 box 0 0 0  6 0 6  sand      # from..to inclusive, then material
                 v 3 1 3 palm                # a single voxel
                 """);
             </code>
            
             Coordinates: x to the right, y UP from the base, z into the scene. Every
             voxel fills the unit cube from (x, y, z) to (x+1, y+1, z+1). Duplicate
             voxels at the same cell resolve last-definition-wins, so detail lines can
             override an earlier box fill.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Voxels">
            <summary>The voxels, in definition order (after dedupe).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Materials">
            <summary>The material table; <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Voxel.Material"/> indexes into it.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.MaterialNames">
            <summary>Material names, parallel to <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Materials"/>.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Min">
            <summary>Smallest occupied cell per axis.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Max">
            <summary>Largest occupied cell per axis.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Contains(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>Whether a cell holds a voxel.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.MaterialIndex(System.String)">
            <summary>Index of a material by name (case-insensitive), -1 if unknown.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.FromVoxels(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Voxel},System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelMaterial})">
            <summary>Builds a model from voxels and materials created in code.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel.Parse(System.String)">
            <summary>
            Parses the .vox text format. Directives (case-insensitive, one per line):
            <c>material NAME top=#RRGGBB [front=#RRGGBB] [side=#RRGGBB]</c> (front
            falls back to top, side to front), <c>box x1 y1 z1 x2 y2 z2 MATERIAL</c>
            (inclusive cuboid), <c>v x y z MATERIAL</c> (single voxel). A <c>#</c>
            that does not start a colour begins a comment. Errors carry the line
            number.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera">
            <summary>
            The orthographic isometric camera for voxel models - the third member of the
            camera family, next to <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Camera2D"/> (2D viewport) and
            <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PinholeCamera"/> (perspective rows). Yaw spins the model, pitch
            tilts the view; the defaults match the voxel tools in the pxl-clock repo
            (344/334 = looking slightly down from the right).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.YawDegrees">
            <summary>Rotation around the vertical axis, in degrees.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.PitchDegrees">
            <summary>Tilt of the view, in degrees. 334 looks slightly down; 360 is level.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.Scale">
            <summary>Canvas pixels per voxel.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.PanX">
            <summary>Screen pan in pixels, applied after projection.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.PanY">
            <summary>Screen pan in pixels, applied after projection.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera.LongAxisPan">
            <summary>
            Pan in [-1, 1] along the model's LONGER horizontal axis - the natural
            way to travel across a wide model without knowing its orientation.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight">
            <summary>
            The light for voxel rendering: ambient floor, one directional light with an
            optional tint on the direct part, a hard cast shadow and smooth ambient
            occlusion. Presets cover the useful studio and time-of-day setups; the
            composable route is <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.FromSkyBody(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBodyState,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)"/>, which derives the light from
            the same <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBodyState"/> that already drives the sky - one sun,
            everything agrees.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Ambient">
            <summary>Light that reaches every face regardless of direction, 0..~1.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Direction">
            <summary>Direction TOWARD the light source (y up). Normalised internally.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Intensity">
            <summary>Strength of the directional part.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Tint">
            <summary>Colour of the direct light; ambient stays neutral.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Shadows">
            <summary>Whether voxels cast hard shadows onto each other.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.AmbientOcclusion">
            <summary>Whether corners and creases darken (the "clay model" look).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.StudioRight">
            <summary>Neutral studio light from the right - the default.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.StudioLeft">
            <summary>Neutral studio light from the left.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Noon">
            <summary>High sun, short shadows.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Golden">
            <summary>Low warm side light, long shadows.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Overcast">
            <summary>Bright, almost shadowless daylight.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.Moonlit">
            <summary>Dim blue night light.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight.FromSkyBody(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBodyState,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double)">
            <summary>
            Derives the light from a sky body sampled by <see cref="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.SkyBody.At(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.DayCycle)"/>:
            horizontal direction from where the body stands, elevation from its
            altitude, warmth from how low it is. Drive the sky and the voxels from
            the SAME body and the scene stays one world.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelRenderExtensions">
             <summary>
             Renders a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel"/> through an <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera"/>:
             orthographic projection, per-face painter sorting, Lambert light with hard
             shadows and smooth ambient occlusion. The maths matches the voxel tools in
             the pxl-clock repo, so a model tuned there looks the same on the panel.
            
             Rendering re-sorts every visible face, so for a static shot bake the result
             once (<see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.BakedSurface"/>) instead of drawing the model every frame.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelRenderExtensions.DrawVoxModel(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight,System.Double,System.Func{Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Color})">
            <summary>
            Draws the model onto the surface, composited over whatever is there.
            The model is centred on the canvas (plus camera pan); <paramref name="shade"/>
            hooks the finished face colour, e.g. <c>c => fog.Apply(c, wz, ...)</c>.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelRenderExtensions.ToMask(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera,System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            The model's projected silhouette as a <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Mask"/> - the entry to
            rim light, halo and drop shadow without knowing anything about voxels.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelRenderExtensions.ToTargets(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera,System.Int32,System.Int32,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelLight)">
            <summary>
            The rendered model as particle targets - so a voxel scene can assemble
            from dust or fall apart into it (<see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.PixelAssembly"/>).
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxelRenderExtensions.Project(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.VoxModel,Pxl.Ui.CSharp.IsoCamera,System.Double,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Projects a point in voxel coordinates to the screen - the bridge from
            the model's world to 2D overlays: a glow on a lamp, a marker, a label
            that follows a voxel while the camera moves. Depth grows away from the
            camera, so overlays can decide in front / behind.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation">
             <summary>
             Falling precipitation as a stateless layer: every drop or flake is derived
             from its index and the current time, so nothing has to be stored, nothing
             drifts out of sync, and the layer can be dropped in front of any scene.
            
             Rain, snow, ash, sparks and confetti are all this class with different
             numbers.
             </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Count">
            <summary>How many particles are in the air at once.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Speed">
            <summary>Fall speed in pixels per second.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.SpeedSpread">
            <summary>Random speed spread (0 = all equal, 1 = between half and double).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Wind">
            <summary>Sideways drift in pixels per second - the wind.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Sway">
            <summary>How far a particle sways sideways around its path.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.SwaySpeed">
            <summary>How fast the sway oscillates.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Streak">
            <summary>Streak length in pixels. 0 draws single pixels (snow), 2-4 gives rain.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Color">
            <summary>
            Particle colour. Derive it from the scene's <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Lighting"/> each
            frame (<c>rain.Color = light.Apply(baseColor, minAmbient)</c>), so the
            weather sits IN the scene instead of glowing on top of it at night.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Alpha">
            <summary>Alpha of the closest particles.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.DepthSpread">
            <summary>
            Depth layering: particles get a random depth in [0,1]; far ones are
            slower and dimmer. 0 disables it and everything falls at the same rate.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Seed">
            <summary>Seed - change it for a different pattern.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.FloorY">
            <summary>Optional row where particles stop (a water line, a roof, the ground).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.FloorFarY">
            <summary>
            Perspective floor: FAR particles (small depth) stop at this row - the
            horizon end of a water surface. Pair with <see cref="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.FloorNearY"/> and
            the rain lands ON the receding surface instead of falling past it.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.FloorNearY">
            <summary>Perspective floor for the NEAREST particles - the bottom of the surface.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Splash">
            <summary>
            Impact length in pixels of fall: after touching its floor a particle
            leaves a brief widening blip before it disappears - the splash that
            sells "it lands there". 0 disables it.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double)">
            <summary>Draws the layer for a point in time.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Weather">
            <summary>
            Ready-made weather layers. They are plain <see cref="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.Precipitation"/> objects -

        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FogBank">
            <summary>
            A drifting bank of fog or cloud: a noise field, faded in at the edges of a
            band, moving sideways. It is the cheapest way to put ATMOSPHERE between the
            viewer and a scene - depth without any geometry.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.FogBank.CenterY">

            <summary>Draws the bank over whatever is on the surface.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="T:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField">
            <summary>
            A night sky: sparse, stable, gently twinkling stars, with a shape mix so the
            sky does not read as uniform noise. Stars are placed by hash, so they never
            flicker or crawl between frames.
            </summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.Density">
            <summary>Fraction of pixels that carry a star.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.Brightness">
            <summary>Overall brightness multiplier.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.TwinkleSpeed">
            <summary>Twinkle speed in radians per second. Keep it low for a wall display.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.TwinkleDepth">
            <summary>How much a star dims between its brief flares (0 = no twinkle).</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.RayBrightness">
            <summary>Brightness of ray pixels relative to the centre.</summary>
        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.ShapeWeights">

        </member>
        <member name="P:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.Color">

        <member name="M:Pxl.Ui.CSharp.StarField.Draw(Pxl.Ui.CSharp.RasterSurface,System.Double,System.Double,System.Int32)">
            <summary>
            Draws the stars into the rows above <paramref name="maxY"/>, faded by

</doc>
